overview.title: Attention matrix, learned projections, query/key/value
overview.main_topic: Completing dot_product_attention with the weighted sum, visualizing the full attention matrix (figure 15.5), making attention richer with Dense projections, and renaming the inputs query, key and value.
overview.central_idea: The weighted sum "bts,bsd->btd" completes dot-product attention. Adding Dense projections of target and source lets the model learn a shared space in which useful source vectors land close to the target, and the general form sum(score(query, key) * value) borrows its vocabulary from search: a query is matched against keys to retrieve values.
overview.importance: This page introduces the query/key/value terminology used everywhere in Transformer literature and code, and the idea that attention needs its own trainable parameters (the four Dense layers).

summary:
The page opens with the last line of `dot_product_attention`: `return np.einsum("bts,bsd->btd", scores, source)`, which, as the callout says, **computes a weighted sum of all source vectors for each target vector**, followed by the call `dot_product_attention(target, source)`.

**Figure 15.5** displays the attention scores as a 2-D matrix when both target and source are sequences. Columns are the English words "I", "will", "bring", "the", "bag", "to", "you"; rows are the Spanish tokens being predicted (in green) "Te", "traeré", "la", "bolsa", "[end]", plus two empty rows. Darker cells are higher scores: "Te" is darkest at "you", "traeré" at "I", "will" and "bring", "la" at "the", "bolsa" at "bag", while "[end]" spreads mid-grey over the last words.

Next, the authors make attention richer by **giving it parameters**. Projecting both source and target vectors with `Dense` layers lets the model find a **shared space** where source vectors are close to target vectors when that helps prediction. The source vectors should also be projected into a separate space before they are combined, and the result projected once more after the summation.

They then adopt the standard names. What they wrote is roughly `sum(score(target, source) * source)`; equivalently, `sum(score(query, key) * value)`. The three-argument version is more general, since in rare cases the vector used to score a source input may differ from the vector that gets summed. The terms come from **search engines and recommender systems**: in a photo search, the query is the search term, the keys are photo tags matched against it, and the values are the photos themselves (figure 15.6, p.466). The page ends by starting the parameterized pseudocode, creating four layers: `query_dense`, `key_dense`, `value_dense` and `output_dense`, each `layers.Dense(dim)`. The function that uses them is on p.466.

paragraphs.excerpt: We can make the hypothesis space of this attention mechanism much richer if we
paragraphs.what_it_says: The hypothesis space of attention becomes richer if the model has parameters to control the score. Projecting both source and target vectors with Dense layers lets the model find a shared space where source vectors are close to target vectors when that improves prediction. The source vectors should also be projected into a separate space before being combined, and once again after the summation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Plain dot-product attention can only use similarities that already exist in the GRU outputs. With learned projections $W_q$ and $W_k$, the score becomes $(W_q t)\cdot(W_k s)$, so the model can learn what "relevant" means for the task, for example making a Spanish verb's vector align with its English subject even if their raw vectors are dissimilar. A third projection $W_v$ chooses what information each source token contributes, and an output projection mixes the combined result.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These four projections are exactly the query, key, value and output Dense layers that appear in the code at the bottom of the page and in every Transformer attention layer.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: $(W_q t)^\top (W_k s) = t^\top (W_q^\top W_k) s$, so learning two projections amounts to learning a (low-rank, if the projection dimension is small) bilinear similarity $t^\top M s$ instead of the fixed identity $t^\top s$.

paragraphs.what_it_says: A different naming has become standard. What was written is roughly sum(score(target, source) * source); it will be written equivalently as sum(score(query, key) * value). This three-argument version is more general: in rare cases you might not want to use the same vector to score source inputs as you use to sum them.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The source plays two roles in the formula: it is compared with the target (key role) and it is what gets blended (value role). Naming them separately allows them to differ. In the translation case query = target and key = value = source, which is how the function is called on p.466.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Query, key and value are the names used by the Keras MultiHeadAttention layer (p.468) and by virtually all Transformer code and papers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In matrix form: $\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top)V$, where the rows of $Q$ are queries and the rows of $K$ and $V$ are keys and values for the same positions.

paragraphs.excerpt: The terminology comes from search engines and recommender systems.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The terminology comes from search engines and recommender systems. In a photo search tool, the query is your search term, the keys are the photo tags matched against the query, and the values are the photos themselves (figure 15.6). The attention mechanism is roughly analogous to this lookup.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A search engine scores how well each key matches the query and returns the corresponding values, ranked. Attention does a soft version: it scores every key against the query, normalizes the scores with softmax, and returns a weighted blend of all values rather than a ranked list.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The analogy makes the separate roles intuitive: you match on tags (keys) but you want the photos (values).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: attention is sometimes called a "differentiable dictionary lookup": a hard lookup returns the value whose key equals the query; attention returns $\sum_j \operatorname{softmax}_j(q\cdot k_j)\,v_j$, which is differentiable in the query, keys and values.

terminology.meaning: A system that ranks items for a user by matching user and item representations.

concepts.name: Query, key and value
concepts.definition: The three inputs of attention: queries are scored against keys, and the scores weight a sum of values: sum(score(query, key) * value).
concepts.intuition: A photo search: the search term (query) is matched against tags (keys), and you get the photos (values).
concepts.technical: $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top)V$; in translation, query = target, key = value = source.
concepts.significance: Standard terminology in all Transformer work; the Keras MultiHeadAttention layer takes query, key and value arguments.
concepts.example: Query "dogs on the beach" matches the key tags Beach + Dog best (figure 15.6).
concepts.misconception: Keys and values are not always different tensors; in most uses they come from the same sequence, projected differently.

concepts.name: Parameterized attention
concepts.definition: Attention with learned Dense projections of the query, key and value inputs and of the output.
concepts.intuition: Let the model learn what to compare and what to retrieve, rather than relying on raw vector similarity.
concepts.significance: It enlarges the hypothesis space of attention.
concepts.example: Four layers.Dense(dim) layers: query_dense, key_dense, value_dense, output_dense.

concepts.name: Attention score matrix
concepts.definition: With target and source sequences, a 2-D matrix in which each row shows the scores for the target word being predicted.
concepts.intuition: A heatmap of which input word each output word looked at.
concepts.technical: Shape (t, s) per example; rows sum to 1 after softmax.
concepts.example: Row "la" is darkest at "the"; row "bolsa" at "bag".

deeper.title: Reading figure 15.5 row by row
deeper.body:
Approximate reading of the heatmap (darker = higher score):

- **"Te"** (to you): darkest at "you", with a dark cell at "I". "Te" is the object pronoun for "you".
- **"traeré"** (I will bring): dark at "I", "will" and "bring", the three words it translates.
- **"la"** (the): black at "the".
- **"bolsa"** (bag): darkest at "bag".
- **"[end]"**: mid-grey spread over "the", "bag", "to", "you", the end of the sentence.

Note (not in the book): Spanish word order differs from English ("Te traeré la bolsa" vs. "I will bring the bag to you"), so the bright cells are not on a diagonal; attention lets the model reorder freely. The two empty rows at the bottom are not explained on the page; they plausibly correspond to padded target positions with no prediction.

deeper.title: Why separate keys from values?
deeper.body: In the photo-search analogy, matching a query against the pixels of every photo would be hard; matching against short tags is easy. But you want the photo, not its tags. Keys are optimized for matching and values for content. In attention, separate key and value projections let one source token advertise itself with one vector ("I am a subject pronoun") while contributing another (its meaning and features).

deeper.title: Counting parameters
deeper.body: Beyond the book: if the input vectors have size $d_{in}$ and each Dense has `dim` units with bias, the query, key and value layers each have $d_{in}\cdot\text{dim} + \text{dim}$ parameters, and output_dense has $\text{dim}\cdot\text{dim} + \text{dim}$. For $d_{in} = \text{dim} = 256$: $4 \times (65{,}536 + 256) = 263{,}168$ parameters, all in the projections, since the score itself has none.

misconceptions.claim: Query, key and value must be three different sequences.
misconceptions.correction: In the translation case, key and value are both the source; in self-attention (p.468) all three are the same sequence. The three-argument form just allows them to differ.

misconceptions.claim: Adding Dense layers changes how the scores are normalized.
misconceptions.correction: The softmax and weighted sum are unchanged; the projections only change which vectors are compared and summed.

takeaways: np.einsum("bts,bsd->btd", scores, source) computes a weighted sum of source vectors for each target vector.
With target and source sequences, attention scores form a 2-D matrix, one row per predicted word (figure 15.5).
Dense projections of target and source give attention parameters and a richer hypothesis space.
sum(score(target, source) * source) is generalized to sum(score(query, key) * value).
The terms come from search: the query is matched to keys to retrieve values.

questions.question: In np.einsum("bts,bsd->btd", scores, source), which axis is summed over?
questions.explanation: s appears in both inputs but not in the output, so it is multiplied and summed: a weighted sum over source positions. b, t and d all survive in btd.

questions.question: In the photo-search analogy, what are the query, the keys and the values?
questions.answer: The query is the search term, the keys are the photo tags matched against the query, and the values are the photos themselves.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph on terminology (and drawn in figure 15.6).

questions.question: Why does projecting the target and source vectors with Dense layers make attention more expressive?
questions.answer: Without projections, the score can only use whatever similarity already exists between the raw vectors. With learned projections, the model can find a shared space where source vectors that help prediction are close to the target, learning what "relevant" means.
questions.explanation: The book calls this making the hypothesis space richer.

questions.question: Why is the three-argument form sum(score(query, key) * value) more general than sum(score(target, source) * source)?
options: It allows the vector used for scoring to differ from the vector that is summed
It removes the need for softmax
It makes attention run over a loop
It allows several targets to share one score
questions.answer: It allows the vector used for scoring to differ from the vector that is summed
questions.explanation: The book says in rare cases you might not want to use the same vector to score as to sum. Softmax is still used, there are no loops, and per-target scores remain.

questions.question: In figure 15.5, which English word does the row for "la" attend to most, and why does that make sense?
questions.answer: "the": "la" is the Spanish feminine article that translates "the".
questions.explanation: The cell ("la", "the") is the darkest in that row. Similarly "bolsa" attends most to "bag".

questions.question: If scores has shape (16, 9, 12) and source has shape (16, 12, 128), what shape does the return line produce, and what does each output vector represent?
questions.answer: (16, 9, 128): for each of 16 examples and each of 9 target positions, a 128-d weighted sum of the 12 source vectors.
questions.explanation: s = 12 is summed out; b, t and d remain.

questions.question: Can you name the role of each of the four Dense layers created at the bottom of the page?
questions.answer: query_dense projects the target for scoring; key_dense projects the source for scoring; value_dense projects the source before it is combined; output_dense projects the result after the summation.
questions.explanation: These map directly onto the sentence "project the source vectors into an entirely separate space before they are combined and once again after the summation".
